## Research Overview: What Hybrid Work Does to Workers (and Their Bosses)

When executives debate whether hybrid remote work helps or hurts, they are often arguing past each other. Three rigorous studies — a large-scale randomized control trial in *Nature*, an industry-level productivity analysis from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and field evidence on perception shifts — have converged on a clear set of findings: **hybrid work (2 days remote / 3 days in-office) does not damage performance but significantly improves employee retention, job satisfaction, and willingness to stay** — while also reshaping how managers *perceive* the arrangement.

Below I present the key studies, synthesize their methods and results, then critically evaluate the limitations, generalizability, and practical implications.

---

## Study 1: The Trip.com Experiment (Bloom, Han & Liang, 2024)

**Full citation:** Bloom N, Han R, Liang J. *Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance*. Nature. 2024;630:920–925. Published June 12, 2024. Open access (doi available via nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07500-2).

### Design & Methods

This was a **six-month randomized control trial** (August 2021 – January 2022) conducted at Trip.com, the third-largest global travel agent by sales in 2019 (NASDAQ-listed, ~35,000 employees, headquartered in Shanghai). The study randomised **1,612 graduate employees** in the Airfare and IT divisions — spanning 395 managers and 1,217 non-managers across software engineering, marketing, accounting, and finance — by even/odd birth date into one of two conditions:

- **Treatment:** Eligible to work from home Wednesdays and Fridays (2 hybrid remote days).
- **Control:** Required in-office five days per week.

Employees were first surveyed on baseline beliefs about WFH's productivity impact, then the experiment ran for six months. An end-line survey measured updated beliefs. Attrition, performance review grades, promotion rates, and lines-of-code submissions (for engineers) were tracked for up to two years post-experiment start. Null equivalence tests (TOST procedure with defined smallest effect sizes of interest) were used to evaluate "null" findings rigorously.
